title: Logs, metrics or traces?

rows.label: In one line
values: Timestamped records of events
Numbers aggregated over time
One request’s path through the services, as timed spans

rows.label: One unit of data
values: A text line or JSON object per event
A sample of a labelled time series, such as a counter, gauge or histogram
A span: trace ID, parent span ID, name, start, duration, status

rows.label: Best at answering
values: What exactly happened to this request, and why?
How much, how fast, and is it getting worse?
Where did the time go, and which hop failed?

rows.label: Cost grows with
values: Traffic and verbosity: GB ingested, stored and scanned
The number of series (label combinations), not traffic
Traffic times spans per request, unless you sample

rows.label: Sampling
values: Drop DEBUG and noisy repeats; keep every error
Not needed: the data is already aggregated
The norm: head (a fixed share) or tail (keep errors and slow traces)

rows.label: Alerting
values: Possible through log-based metrics or queries; slower and costlier
The usual basis for alerts and SLOs
Rarely on traces themselves; on metrics derived from spans

rows.label: Breaks when
values: Lines are free text, or share no ID, so ten services’ logs can’t be joined
A label has unbounded values, or someone averages percentiles
One service in the path doesn’t pass the header on, so the trace splits

rows.label: Standards
values: Syslog (RFC 5424); OpenTelemetry log data model
Prometheus exposition format; StatsD; OpenTelemetry metrics
W3C Trace Context; OpenTelemetry traces

rows.label: Joins to the others by
values: `trace_id` and `span_id` fields on each line
Exemplars: sample values that carry a trace ID
The trace ID, which finds the logs; span data can produce rate, error and duration metrics

rows.label: Where it’s stored
values: CloudWatch Logs, Cloud Logging, Azure Monitor Logs, Loki, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, ClickStack
Prometheus, CloudWatch metrics, Cloud Monitoring, Azure Monitor Metrics
X-Ray, Cloud Trace, Application Insights, Jaeger, Zipkin, ClickStack

tip: You need all three, in this order: metrics to notice (alert on rate, errors and duration), traces to find the slow or failing hop, and logs for the details of that one request. Make them join from the start: the same service name everywhere and the trace ID in every log line.
